````markdown
# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. It is good advice, and it asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them.

There is another way to get the weekend back. In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference. Still, the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves.

A tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table sorting paper. The tin does not have to become a Friday chore. It can become somebody else's job.

This January, the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does.
````

content.content:
## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.

# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. It is good advice, and it asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them.

In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday. "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea," she says. She photographs each receipt when she gets it, and a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

This January, the tin could stay on the shelf.
EOF

**1. False statements**

- **"Only 'This January' points ahead."** (finding 6, about the delivered text). The delivered text also has "The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January", which points ahead to the coming deadline. So "This January" is not the only forward reference. The statement should name the deadline sentence, or say only that nothing gives a reason why this year in particular.

- **"The piece keeps to the weekly habit as what makes January short."** (Brief fulfilment 5, about the delivered text). The delivered text says the opposite: "The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference." It does not present the weekly habit as the cause of a short January. The reply says so itself under question 9: "The text does not say the habit causes the shorter return, because the survey does not show cause." What is true is that the text puts the weekly habit next to the lower reported median (6 hours against 19) and makes no claim of cause.

**2. Claim changes the account misses**

- **The headline's claim moved though its wording did not.** "# Ten minutes on a Friday" is the same in both texts.
  - As it arrived, nothing in the body mentioned ten minutes. The headline could only be read as a picture of the weekly Friday habit, and the body then set that habit aside for an accountant ("It can become somebody else's job").
  - As delivered, the headline names Priya's session, "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea", and states what the piece recommends.
  - A changed claim is accounted for by what it now asserts, not by how far its wording moved. The account says nothing about the headline except "The heading and the first three paragraphs are word for word as they arrived", and it ends with "No other claim was removed, changed or added."

- **The new order adds a framing and an implied cause.**
  - Before: "There is another way to get the weekend back. In a survey this summer, 412 of our users…"
  - After: "In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday. … She photographs each receipt when she gets it…" followed straight away by "In a survey this summer, 412 of our users… Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours…" and then the new ending "This January, the tin could stay on the shelf."
  - Coming right after Priya's paragraph, the survey now reads as evidence for her Friday habit. It puts her among the weekly matchers with the 6-hour median, and it presents the habit as what lets the tin stay on the shelf. That is an ordering, an actor and a causal framing that the arrived text did not have.
  - The account treats the reordering as outside the claims: "Apart from the claims listed above, the run also restructured the second half. A paragraph on Priya's Friday session now comes before the survey figures…" For the ending it records only that it "now says, still as a possibility, that this January the tin could stay on the shelf." It does not say that the ending now rests on the weekly habit, or that the survey is now framed as support for Priya's example.
